newsitem.title: UK: Britain's mid-size ad agencies follow merger cycle.
newsitem.headline: Britain's mid-size ad agencies follow merger cycle.

text.p: As sure as spring turns into summer, Britain's mid-sized advertising agencies are following their own seasons and merging with their larger brothers -- insuring growth and survival in a world where bigger is usually better.
The recent announcement by London-based Simons Palmer Clemmow Johnson that it would merge into TBWA, a global ad agency owned by Omnicom Group Inc, only confirmed the cycle goes on.
"It's as regular as clockwork," said Rupert Howell, a partner in Howell Henry Chaldecott Lury, another London-based mid-sized agency. "There are lots of start-ups. Some of them fail.

"But those that don't fail, they get to a medium size and then you are left with two choices," Howell said. "It is impossible to get from middle size to big unless you have a strong competitive difference."

Bob Willott, a principal in Willott Kingston Smith, an accountancy firm with an advertising industry specialty, called the Simons Palmer deal "absolutely predictable." In an industry where new agencies are sown with regularity, there is a cycle of agencies being absorbed into larger networks and disappearing over time.
"It doesn't mean that everybody else will go the same way," Willott said. "But I think there will be fewer in the middle ground."
"In advertising all you need is one person, a telephone and a desk," said Howell. "So the barriers to entry are very, very low. ... Every five years there are lots of start-ups."
But few agencies are able to continue independently if they want to make it into the big leagues.

While Simons Palmer was a respected ad agency, it lacked the strong competitive difference needed for it to make the next leap, Howell said. Paul Simons, himself, one of the agencies partners and named as chief executive of the merged TBWA/Simons Palmer group, has said that the agency was facing a glass ceiling -- unable to win accounts worth more than five million pounds.

Howell insisted his own agency can buck the trend and continue to go it alone, as can mid-sized rival Bartle Bogle Hegarty. "The two of us do not need to sell, and hopefully we will grow into very big agencies," he said.
Behind the need for mid-sized agencies to tie their fortunes to large networks is the increasing globalisation of businesses.
"Inevitably, if you look at other industries, globalisation has become the norm," said David Miles, an advertising analyst with Deloitte Touche Ross.

Miles Colebrook, group president, international, of WPP Group Plc's J. Walter Thompson ad agency, echoed the sentiment. "Look at airlines, look at what's happened to accountancy firms, legal firms," he said.
Some argue globalisation is not a driving force in ad agency mergers because few ad campaigns are designed on an international, or even pan-European, scale.
Colebrook, however, said, "More and more the strategic thinking is global, and you've got to remember that a lot of what agenices do is the strategic work and not just producing campaigns.
"Campaigns are still inclined to be regional ones, local ones, and I think that will continue," he said. But companies with global brands want global partners.
A global ad agency network means "no more reinventing the wheel," Colebrook said. "Great ideas from Japan move to Latin America in weeks rather than years."
On the other side of the equation lie the big agencies, driven to acquire their mid-sized competitors by the need to fill out their global networks and acquire talent.
